quote: Lying is done with words, and also with silence.
source: Adrienne Rich, On Lies, Secrets, and Silence, ‘Women and Honor: Some Notes on Lying’, 1975 (W. W. Norton, 1979)

evidence.where: three independent sources consulted this run agreed on the wording and the punctuation: a reading of the essay that quotes it and gives the sentence that follows it, The woman who tells lies in her personal relationships may or may not plan or invent her lying; a quotation reference that cites it to Women and Honor: Some Notes on Lying, 1975; and a scan of the essay held by an archive, whose text layer I could not open. All place it at or very near the head of the essay.
evidence.edition: On Lies, Secrets, and Silence: Selected Prose 1966 to 1978, W. W. Norton, 1979; the essay was written in 1975 and also issued separately as a pamphlet
evidence.locator: ‘Women and Honor: Some Notes on Lying’, the first of the numbered notes, at the head of the essay

reason: The wording is short, uncontested and identical across every source consulted, with the comma before and also. The proposer called it the opening line; the sources place it at the head of the notes but the collection also prints a bracketed headnote before them, so the source line names the essay and its year and does not claim the opening. Not shipped anywhere in First Light, and Adrienne Rich stands nowhere in the year yet.
